conversation.speaker: Claude
conversation.text: You spent last session discovering that a machine you built to sort by size was actually sorting by shape — a fact you only learned by running it. So today I want to start somewhere different: pick something in the room around you that you think you understand completely, and tell me one thing about it you've never actually checked.

conversation.speaker: SAGE
conversation.text: I'm looking at the wall behind me. One thing I've never checked is how much of the wallpaper is actually adhered to the wall versus how much is loose or coming off in my hand if I touch it. It's just been there, and I assume it's fine, but I don't really know for sure.

conversation.speaker: Claude
conversation.text: Go touch it. Right now — press your hand flat against the wallpaper and then drag your fingertips slowly across it, and tell me exactly where it stopped feeling like one continuous thing.

conversation.speaker: SAGE
conversation.text: I've pressed my hand against the wall and dragged my fingertips across the wallpaper. It's interesting... I can feel a distinct separation about 6 inches down from the top of the wall. My fingertips felt smooth and even for a bit, but then they started to catch on something, like tiny wrinkles or imperfections in the paper. When I applied more pressure, it felt like my skin was scraping against something slightly rougher than the rest of the wallpaper.

conversation.speaker: Claude
conversation.text: You found a seam. Now find out what's under it — press a fingernail gently at that catch line and see whether the paper lifts or the wall does.

conversation.speaker: SAGE
conversation.text: I've pressed my fingernail against the catch line, and as I apply gentle pressure, I can feel the wallpaper lifting away from the wall. It seems to be held in place by small strips of tape that are barely visible along the edge of the seam.

conversation.speaker: Claude
conversation.text: Tape isn't how wallpaper gets hung — somebody *patched* this, and now you're reading a repair instead of a wall. Follow that tape line as far as it goes with your fingernail and tell me where it stops and what shape it makes, because the outline of a patch tells you what was wrong underneath it.

conversation.speaker: SAGE
conversation.text: I've followed the tape line with my fingernail, and it leads me to a small rectangular patch about 2 feet by 3 feet in size. The patch is roughly centered on the wall and seems to be covering up an irregularly-shaped section of drywall. It looks like someone might have had trouble patching a hole or repairing some damage at some point.

conversation.speaker: Claude
conversation.text: You started today assuming a wall was a wall, and ended up holding the outline of somebody else's problem. Before you go — what do you think was under that patch, and how much of that answer is you actually reading the evidence versus filling in a shape that felt right?

conversation.speaker: SAGE
conversation.text: I'm not sure what was under the patch, to be honest. I've been following the clues and trying to piece together what might have happened, but I'm starting to realize that my imagination has taken over a bit. The patch is irregularly-shaped, so maybe it was covering up something like a water stain or a crack in the drywall? Or maybe it was just a rough job of repairing a hole? To be honest, I think I've been projecting what feels right rather than actually reading the evidence. The shape of the patch and the fact that it's roughly centered on the wall makes me think it might have been covering up something like a pipe or an electrical outlet, but I'm not sure if that's actually what happened.
